A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AccNet research, with matching authors, architectures and compositional-learning framework. The text, equations, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data learning curves, differentiability sweeps, WESAD classification results and network singular-value analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and WESAD experiments, adds MNIST results, and numerically compares generalization bounds.

M1.justification: Appendix A.2 changes the reported training cost from L1 to L2, accompanying the MSE setup. Section 2.1 also describes an optional output contraction to enforce bounded predictions. The AccNet architecture, ResNet extension, SVD correspondence and two complexity regularizers are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix A.1.2 and Figure 1 add MNIST, extending evaluation into ten-class handwritten-digit image classification. This introduces a distinct domain and task beyond the retained synthetic compositional regression and WESAD binary stress classification.

E2.justification: New Figure 4 numerically compares bounds labeled Neyshabur15, Bartlett17, Neyshabur18 and Ledent21 against the proposed bounds; v1 has no corresponding comparison. Figure 2 also adds FCNN to the differentiability-rate heatmaps, although FCNN/DNN already participated in v1 Figure 1.

E3.justification: Appendix A changes the synthetic training/test split from 20,000/2,000 to 50,000/2,500 and extends the training-size sweep to 50,000. The stated cost changes from L1 to L2, and Figure 1 changes the illustrated smoothness pairs. New Figure 4 omits bound prefactors and estimates Lipschitz constants using 100 random points.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds a focused mechanism analysis comparing operator-norm and sampled-Jacobian versions of the bound across four smoothness combinations, including the regime where both component functions are difficult. The existing differentiability-sensitivity and singular-value analyses are retained, with revised results and presentation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v1 explicitly acknowledges absent error bars in its checklist; v2 adds qualitative noise cautions without introducing statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The scaling curves, heatmaps and singular-value plots change, while MNIST results and numerical comparisons with prior bounds are added. Section 3.2 changes the reported bound-to-error gap from roughly 10^3 to 10^7. Changed losses, sample sizes and illustrated smoothness settings prevent interpreting these differences as same-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the Lipschitz-loss generalization-gap analysis with square-root-MSE bounds, adds Appendix B concentration results, and rederives the Sobolev and regularized-minimizer rates. Section 4.2.2 adds a computational-graph extension. Several approximation lemmas are retained under renumbering. Appendix D's Theorem 12, however, retains a ratio definition inconsistent with its revised proof and main Theorem 4.

C1.justification: Section 1.1 materially redefines the central guarantee: v1 claims a bounded-Lipschitz-loss gap proportional to R log(N)/sqrt(N), whereas v2 claims an MSE square-root-loss bound with corresponding risk guarantees when training error is small. The overarching compositionality and symmetry-learning claims in the abstract and conclusion remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of F1 versus other norms, norm-based versus sparsity-based guarantees, the N^-1/2 rate ceiling, and implicit Lipschitz control through training stability. It revises the claimed depth penalty for the second regularizer and adds qualifications about rank assumptions, potentially artificial rate terms and noisy empirical comparisons.

D1.justification: Figure 4 documents the 100-point Lipschitz approximation and omission of prefactors. Appendix A updates synthetic GPU time from 6.3 to approximately seven days, adds MNIST compute information, and removes the specific CPU model. The code link and most architecture, optimizer and training-schedule details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The introduction and Sections 3.2–4.2 substantially expand positioning against existing norm bounds and sparsity-based compositional-learning results. Added works include Golowich et al., Galanti et al. on compositional sparsity, Poggio and Fraser, Srebro et al., and Cohen et al. The revision explains specific differences in norms, depth dependence and attainable rates.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten and Section 4.2 reorganized into explicit discussions of norms, sparsity, Lipschitz constants, depth and limitations, followed by dedicated experimental and computational-graph subsections. The appendices are reorganized around a new covering-number section, the NeurIPS checklist is removed, and 'modulo map' becomes 'quotient map'.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 2–3 are reorganized into a six-panel Figure 2 with different colormaps and comparison panels. Figure 1 combines MNIST and WESAD, the singular-value figure moves from Figure 4 to Figure 3, and a new bound-comparison Figure 4 appears. The ICLR template also changes headings, headers and the author block throughout.

improvement.justification: The MSE-specific analysis, direct comparisons with prior bounds and clearer qualifications of near-optimality make v2 more informative and easier to assess. These benefits are tempered by new internal inconsistencies: Appendix D's Theorem 12 retains min(nu/d), while its proof and main Theorem 4 use max(d/nu). The added experiments also lack quantified uncertainty and detailed MNIST protocols. The net improvement is therefore limited despite the substantial revision.
